article_title: School Reform, Retention Policy, and Student Achievement Gains
citation: Stuart Luppescu, Anthony S. Bryk, Paul Deabster, John Q. Easton, and Yeow Meng Thum. (1995). School Reform, Retention Policy, and Student Achievement Gains. University of Chicago draft report.
title: Do not rely on grade retention to help lagging students catch up, since promoted comparable students make larger gains
description: The article concludes that if retention's purpose is to let lagging students catch up, its results indicate the opposite effect: promoted students out-gain comparable retained students, so retention leaves students falling further behind. This is the authors' policy conclusion drawn from their matched propensity comparisons of achievement gains in Chicago elementary schools.
requirements: Comparisons should match retained and promoted students on a propensity for retention so the groups are comparable
constraints: The finding comes from one district's 1987-1992 data, with third grade a notable exception and the gain difference averaging about one-quarter of a logit
target_learners: Elementary students at risk of grade retention
target_learning_goals: Improving annual achievement gains in reading and mathematics
examples: The study compared gains of retained versus promoted students within cohorts (diagonal comparisons) and of first-time versus repeating grade-takers (vertical comparisons), finding promoted students ahead in almost all cases
key_sources: Stuart Luppescu, Anthony S. Bryk, Paul Deabster, John Q. Easton, and Yeow Meng Thum. (1995). School Reform, Retention Policy, and Student Achievement Gains. University of Chicago draft report. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/school-reform-retention-policy-and-student-achievement-gains

article_title: AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218
title: Avoid anthropomorphizing AI: refer to AI as it and avoid calling GenAI errors hallucinations
description: Because computers cannot take into account context and emotions, lack consciousness, and are 'not reflective or able to assess its actions,' the report states 'we caution against anthropomorphizing AI.' The authors remind users 'that AI tools should be referred to as "it" rather than pronouns and avoid referencing GenAI errors as "hallucinations" to avoid making light of mental health issues (Ruiz & Glazer, 2024).' This supports the Core Value of Centering Human Judgment by keeping the distinction between human and machine capabilities clear.
requirements: Educators and users maintain the human-machine distinction in language when discussing AI tools with learners
target_learning_goals: center human judgment when using AI
understand limits of AI capabilities
examples: The report cites Ruiz & Glazer (2024) for the recommendation to avoid the term hallucinations
key_sources: Mills, K., Ruiz, P., Lee, K., Coenraad, M., Fusco, J., Roschelle, J., & Weisgrau, J. (2024). AI Literacy: A Framework to Understand, Evaluate, and Use Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/218

article_title: The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist
citation: Angela Chen, Siwei Jin, Catherine Bao, Canwen Wang, Robert E. Kraut, Tongshuang Wu, and Haiyi Zhu. (2026). The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist Micro-Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10051
title: Adaptive Virtual Patient framework: separating behavioral state transitions from language generation
description: The AVP framework inserts an explicit behavioral-state module between the trainee's turn and the virtual patient's reply: LLM evaluators score empathy and exploration each turn, a dynamics module accumulates the scores into an ordinal disclosure level (G/M/H) using weights derived from a psychotherapy-data SEM, and an LLM generates the next utterance conditioned on that level. The article argues that "Keeping the behavioral logic separate from generation makes the VP’s adaptation inspectable, controllable, and fixed across experimental conditions in a way a prompt-only system cannot achieve." The level determines what the patient may reveal; the LLM determines how they say it.
requirements: Requires an external data-driven model of interaction dynamics (the SEM of Chen et al., 2026) to parameterize the state-update weights
Requires validated skill detectors scoring user behaviors each turn
constraints: The dynamics module is parameterized from psychotherapy data and encodes assumptions specific to therapeutic communication; broader-domain claims are not yet validated
The deployed 3:1 weight is an integer approximation, not an empirically optimized parameter
target_learners: clinicians and clinical trainees practicing psychotherapy micro-skills
target_learning_goals: empathic responding
exploratory probing
recognizing contingent patient disclosure
examples: In the evaluation, the AVP kept the guarded persona at G-level until accumulated empathy and exploration crossed the M threshold, while the static condition presented H-level topics from turn one
key_sources: Angela Chen, Siwei Jin, Catherine Bao, Canwen Wang, Robert E. Kraut, Tongshuang Wu, and Haiyi Zhu. (2026). The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist Micro-Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10051

article_title: The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist
citation: Angela Chen, Siwei Jin, Catherine Bao, Canwen Wang, Robert E. Kraut, Tongshuang Wu, and Haiyi Zhu. (2026). The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist Micro-Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10051
title: Four measurable properties for evaluating adaptive virtual patients: responsiveness, gradual build-up, faithful realization, and skill sensitivity
description: The article proposes four measurable properties an adaptive virtual patient should satisfy, each with its own metric: P1 Responsiveness (state changes in the direction the data predicts), P2 Gradual Build-up (the state "climbs steadily across the session and only as the user earns it"), P3 Faithful Realization (generated text matches the intended state), and P4 Skill Sensitivity (different users get visibly different sessions). Each property comes with its own metric, so evaluators can locate exactly where a system fails rather than collapse the question into one number.
requirements: Each property requires its own metric: OLS regression for responsiveness, decile-slope fit for build-up, rater agreement for realization, and a median skill split for sensitivity
constraints: The P4 skill-sensitivity interaction test was underpowered at N= 20 per stratum in the article's own evaluation
target_learners: clinicians and clinical trainees practicing psychotherapy micro-skills
target_learning_goals: evaluating whether a simulated patient adapts to trainee behavior
examples: The article operationalized P2 by splitting each session into 10 deciles and fitting a linear slope and R2 across decile-averaged disclosure levels
key_sources: Angela Chen, Siwei Jin, Catherine Bao, Canwen Wang, Robert E. Kraut, Tongshuang Wu, and Haiyi Zhu. (2026). The Empirically Grounded Adaptive Virtual Patient for Psychotherapy Training: Disclosure That Responds to Therapist Micro-Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10051

article_title: Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives
citation: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7
title: Design worked examples to avoid split-attention and redundancy
description: The review reports that early worked-example research showed example study is not always more effective than problem solving and that design plays a crucial role. This yielded guidelines to "avoid split-attention by integrating mutually referring information sources such as text and picture/diagram" and to avoid redundancy, presenting multiple information sources only when both are necessary for comprehension, since an easily-understood-in-isolation source should be left out. Spoken rather than written text can also integrate pictorial information.
requirements: Mutually referring information sources (text and picture/diagram) must be physically or temporally integrated
constraints: Redundant sources should be omitted only when they can be easily understood in isolation
target_learning_goals: learning problem-solving procedures from worked examples
examples: Tarmizi and Sweller's work on split-attention in geometry examples; Mousavi et al. providing spoken rather than written text with pictorial information
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7

article_title: The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention
citation: van Dijk, M., Blom, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2020). The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention. Journal of Intelligence, 8(4), 37. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence8040037
title: Score originality with methods not based on relative response frequency within the sample
description: Because sample-relative originality coding can bias scores when conditions differ in the stimulus array children see, the authors recommend alternative scoring. They state: "we recommend considering alternative ways of coding in future research which are not based on the relative response frequency within the sample, such as using a jury to assess the responses". They also note frequency estimates are more accurate with larger samples and suggest intersubjective rating or automated scoring.
requirements: A scoring method that does not depend on response frequency within the study sample, such as jury rating or automated scoring
constraints: Sample-relative coding may favour conditions in which children's answers draw on idiosyncratic memories rather than a shared stimulus array
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of creative originality
examples: In the study, uses mentioned by less than 10% of the sample were coded as original, and the authors argue this coding may have favoured the low stimulus condition
key_sources: van Dijk, M., Blom, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2020). The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention. Journal of Intelligence, 8(4), 37. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence8040037

article_title: Effects of action video game play on cognitive skills: A meta-analysis
citation: Benoit Bediou, Melissa A. Rodgers, Elizabeth Tipton, Richard E. Mayer, C. Shawn Green, and Daphne Bavelier. (2023). Effects of Action Video Game Play on Cognitive Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Technology, Mind, and Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1037/tmb0000102
title: Learning-to-learn account: action game mechanics train attentional control and enable transfer to nongame contexts
description: The article proposes that the game mechanics inherent in action video games—enemies appearing anywhere in a large field of view, cluttered scenes, and many quickly and independently moving targets—place heavy load on perceptual and attentional skills. The authors "proposed that the game mechanics inherent in action video games may be ideally suited to train core cognitive functions, such as attentional control, and in turn facilitate transfer to nongame contexts (learning to learn)". This framework motivates why intervention studies test transfer to untrained cognitive tasks rather than only in-game improvement.
requirements: Intervention designs must contrast action game training with an active control game and measure untrained cognitive tasks at posttest at least 24 hr after training
constraints: The article defines action video games narrowly as first- and third-person shooters, excluding action-like genres such as action RPGs and MOBAs
target_learning_goals: perception
top-down attentional control
spatial cognition
transfer of cognitive skill to untrained tasks
examples: The intervention meta-analysis tested this account by contrasting commercially available action games with nonaction control games in pre/post designs with a minimum of 8 hr of training over at least 8 sessions
key_sources: Benoit Bediou, Melissa A. Rodgers, Elizabeth Tipton, Richard E. Mayer, C. Shawn Green, and Daphne Bavelier. (2023). Effects of Action Video Game Play on Cognitive Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Technology, Mind, and Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1037/tmb0000102

article_title: An inventory of peer assessment diversity
citation: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444
title: Avoid the term 'co-assessment'; specify how peer and staff assessment relate instead
description: The article advises against the label 'co-assessment' because 'the use of this label, however, masks all details about how teachers' and peers' assessments actually relate to each other'. Instead, the inventory's 'Relationship to other assessments' variable requires specifying whether peer assessment is (partially) substitutional or supplementary, whether re-marking is possible, and, if supplementary, its timing relative to staff assessment and whether parties know each other's judgements.
requirements: Designers must describe the concrete relationship between peer and staff assessment rather than using an umbrella term
constraints: The recommendation applies to designs where students collaborate with staff in assessment; the term is also rejected for designs where students do not take full responsibility
target_learners: students in higher education courses combining peer and staff assessment
target_learning_goals: transparent and comparable description of combined peer–staff assessment arrangements
examples: The article distinguishes substitutional designs where students become 'surrogate' teachers, partially substitutional designs where students act as 'assistant' teachers taking over only part of the assessment, and supplementary designs where peers and staff assess the same performance
key_sources: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444

article_title: The Risks of Rewards. ERIC Digest.
citation: Kohn, Alfie. (1994). The Risks of Rewards. ERIC Digest. ERIC Clearinghouse on Elementary and Early Childhood Education Urbana IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376990
title: Avoid classroom management programs that rely on rewards and consequences; build a caring community that solves problems collaboratively
description: This principle holds that educators who want students to take responsibility for their own behavior and to internalize positive values should not use reward- and consequence-based management programs. The recommended alternative is "creating a caring community whose members solve problems collaboratively and decide together how they want their classroom to be." The digest grounds this in its analysis that rewards and punishments are two sides of the same manipulative coin.
requirements: Educators must prioritize internalization of positive values and student self-responsibility over mindless obedience for the alternative to be worth adopting.
constraints: The digest addresses typical practices in classrooms in the United States; ways rewards are used and values considered important differ among and within cultures.
target_learning_goals: Prosocial values and responsibility
Self-directed learning
examples: The digest cites DeVries & Zan (1994) and Solomon et al. (1992) on constructivist classrooms and caring-community practices as the alternative to bribes and threats.
key_sources: Kohn, Alfie. (1994). The Risks of Rewards. ERIC Digest. ERIC Clearinghouse on Elementary and Early Childhood Education Urbana IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376990

article_title: Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education
citation: Cowan Nelson. (2014). Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4207727/
title: Avoid presenting more than a few items or ideas at once unless they can be rapidly integrated
description: From the summary of what working memory research establishes, the article draws a practical rule: "To avoid overtaxing an individual's working-memory capabilities, one should avoid presenting more than a few items or ideas at once, unless the items can be rapidly integrated." It also advises avoiding making people hold unintegrated information for a very long time, as in sentences that delay the unifying theme.
requirements: Presentations must respect the roughly 3 to 4 chunk capacity limit, or provide rapid integration of items into larger chunks
constraints: The rule applies when learners have limited long-term knowledge of the topic, since expertise allows slots to be filled with complex concepts
target_learning_goals: comprehension of instructions
reading comprehension
concept formation
examples: The article notes teachers must be sensitive to the possibility that part of a two-step instruction to a preschool child may be forgotten before it is carried out
key_sources: Cowan Nelson. (2014). Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4207727/

article_title: Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy
citation: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://www.upenn.edu
title: Avoid critical-period fatalism: contemporary neuroscience does not support sharply defined critical periods, and adult plasticity remains substantial
description: The article argues that emphasis on early sensitive periods in policy discourse can fuel defeatism about helping older children, teens and adults. It responds that "contemporary neuroscience does not support sharply defined critical periods for psychological development, and has only begun to understand age-related changes in plasticity", and that a key recent insight is the plasticity remaining in the adult brain. Earlier intervention may generally be more effective, but expected effectiveness at different ages should inform, not eliminate, resource allocation to older needy populations.
requirements: Policy framing that pairs early-childhood emphasis with continued recognition of later plasticity
constraints: The article acknowledges that with fixed resources, prioritizing earlier interventions may leave older children and adults with less help, and that economists reach a similar earlier-is-better conclusion
target_learners: older children, teens and adults from low socioeconomic status backgrounds
target_learning_goals: maintaining developmental and educational support across the lifespan
examples: The article quotes a critic warning that alarm about irrevocably damaged young brains "can all too easily fuel defeatism" and weaken the case for subsequent help
key_sources: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41583-018-0023-2

article_title: Guiding group cognition in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7
title: Avoid guiding collaboration so externally that it undermines the group's autonomy, agency and sociability
description: The article warns that CSCL researchers "can become focused on trying to promote and control collaboration from outside the group itself." Taken too far, this can foster strategic communication and impression management, furthering external goals at the expense of "the group's own autonomy, agency, and sociability," and students can be influenced to pursue high grades rather than knowledge building. The recommended response is to return to the interpersonal resources of the participants themselves.
requirements: Support for collaboration should preserve the group's own autonomy, agency, and sociability
constraints: Taken too far, external promotion and control of collaboration fosters strategic communication and impression management
target_learning_goals: knowledge building rather than grade-seeking strategies
examples: The editorial closes the issue's reflection by returning to interpersonal resources of group participants, via Gerdes's paper on trust
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7

article_title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
citation: Molenaar, I., Chiu, M. M., Sleegers, P., & van Boxtel, C. (2011). Scaffolding of small groups' metacognitive activities with an avatar. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 601-624. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9130-z
title: Avatar-based metacognitive scaffolding system in the Ontdeknet learning environment
description: A computerized scaffolding system integrated into the Ontdeknet virtual learning environment, in which the avatar David delivers metacognitive scaffolds to triads. Scaffold timing was based on Zimmerman's model of self-regulated learning and on students' attention focus, with a minimum of 12 scaffolds per condition during the first two lessons. Problematizing scaffolds required responses: "The triads in the problematizing condition were obliged to answer the avatar 's questions in an answer box on the screen". Control triads saw the same avatar without scaffolds to control for a Hawthorne effect.
requirements: Scaffolds must be dynamically timed to instances when metacognitive activities are typically executed in the learning process
target_learners: elementary school students in grades four to six
target_learning_goals: planning, monitoring, and evaluating learning during a collaborative country-exploration assignment
examples: Triads worked six hours on the assignment 'Would you like to live abroad?' about New Zealand or Iceland, consulting an expert inhabitant via the environment.
key_sources: Molenaar, I., Chiu, M. M., Sleegers, P., & van Boxtel, C. (2011). Scaffolding of small groups' metacognitive activities with an avatar. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 601-624. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9130-z

article_title: The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning
citation: Lukas Wesenberg, Sebastian Jansen, Felix Krieglstein, Felicia Meusel, Sascha Schneider, Georg Valtin, Günter Daniel Rey. (2026). The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09781-8
title: Avoid large amounts of seductive details in learning materials; small amounts may have negligible effects
description: Because both studies showed a linear negative effect of the seductive detail amount on recall while no effect appeared for transfer, load, or motivation, the article recommends limiting the volume of interesting-but-irrelevant digressions in learning materials. As the authors state, "Especially the inclusion of large amounts of digressions should be avoided by teachers and instructional designers, while the inclusion of small amounts might have rather negligible effects." The recommendation follows from the dose-response pattern rather than from a tested optimum.
requirements: Requires keeping the amount of seductive content low relative to the learning-relevant text (conditions spanning 0%–50% SD text were tested)
constraints: The effect was observed on recall only; transfer showed no significant linear effect and a Study 2 polynomial transfer trend was unstable under cross-validation
target_learners: students in text-based learning environments, from secondary school to university
target_learning_goals: recall of learning-relevant text content
examples: Study 1 embedded 150 or 300 seductive words in a 600-word text and Study 2 embedded 120–480 seductive words in a 960-word text, holding interruptions constant across SD conditions
key_sources: Lukas Wesenberg, Sebastian Jansen, Felix Krieglstein, Felicia Meusel, Sascha Schneider, Georg Valtin, Günter Daniel Rey. (2026). The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09781-8

article_title: Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning?
citation: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z
title: Avoid jangle fallacies: use precise definitions, require added explanatory power for new constructs, and reach measurement consensus
description: The commentary recommends that researchers linking fields be parsimonious with constructs: define constructs precisely, show that allegedly novel constructs have additional explanatory power before introducing them, and reach consensus on measurement. As the article puts it, "Simply inventing new names for the same constructs should be avoided, as it creates unnecessary redundancy (i.e., jangle fallacies)." It cites renamed constructs in the special issue (effort-by-complexity vs. data-driven effort; required mental effort vs. mental load; cognitive demand vs. cognitive load) as examples.
requirements: New constructs must demonstrate additional explanatory power, such as resolving conflicts in empirical data or explaining previously unexplained observations
Community consensus on how key constructs like cognitive load and effort are measured, including critical test scenarios and multiple measures within one paradigm
constraints: Researchers must be aware of the type of appraisals they prompt learners to make, since appraisal wording can affect results; David et al. found no evidence that the formulation of effort appraisals moderated their mediation model
target_learners: education and psychology researchers studying effort and cognitive load
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptualization and measurement of effort and cognitive load constructs
examples: The commentary questions the added benefit of renaming monitoring accuracy as self-assessment accuracy, and of shifting from mental load to required mental effort
key_sources: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z

article_title: Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model
citation: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w
title: Avoid labeling within-domain effects in the classic I/E model as pure social comparison effects
description: The article recommends that researchers avoid interpreting within-domain effects in the classic I/E model as exclusively reflecting social comparisons. The authors state that "labeling the within-domain effects in the classic I/E model as 'social comparison effects', as occasionally done in the literature... should be avoided" because these effects likely also reflect dimensional comparisons, criterion-based comparisons against individual or objective standards, and temporal comparisons. They recommend the more cautious terms "within-domain effects" and "between-domain effects."
requirements: Researchers interpreting I/E model coefficients should consider that multiple comparison processes (social, dimensional, criterion-based, temporal) may contribute to within-domain effects
constraints: This recommendation applies specifically to the interpretation of effects in the classic I/E model parameterization
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of academic self-concept formation processes
examples: The authors use the terms 'within-domain effects' and 'between-domain effects' throughout their six studies rather than 'social comparison effects'
key_sources: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w

article_title: Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades
citation: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6
title: Avoid gender stereotyping in L2 educational practice; cultivate inclusive environments addressing individual needs
description: Because the pooled female advantage is small and highly context-dependent, the article recommends that educators not attribute achievement differences broadly to gender. It states educators "should focus on cultivating inclusive learning environments that address individual needs, encourage participation across all skill domains, and mitigate potential gender biases in instruction and assessment." This guards against stereotype-driven disparities in academic and professional choices.
requirements: Educators and policy makers must treat the small average gap as insufficient grounds for gender-based expectations or tracking in language instruction.
constraints: The recommendation rests on a small effect size (g = 0.17) with very high heterogeneity; the article warns a belief in a female advantage may contribute to disparities in college admissions or special education placements.
target_learners: L2 learners across elementary, secondary, and university settings
target_learning_goals: Second/foreign language achievement across speaking, listening, reading, and writing
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 137 effect sizes and found the advantage diminishes to non-significance at university level, supporting individualized rather than gendered expectations.
key_sources: Chen, X., Zhou, Z., & Padilla, A. M. (2026). Do Females Outperform Males on Second/Foreign Language (L2) Achievement? A Meta-Analytical Review across Three Decades. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10092-6

article_title: Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5
title: Availability to learn is a prerequisite condition, established by a summative ratio of contributors to challenges, that must be met before SRL can activate
description: The article's central framework holds that availability to learn is a prerequisite stage preceding even preparatory phases of SRL process models. Learners weigh and sum psychological and environmental conditions, and "We propose a ratio function when contributors to availability can outweigh detractors and SRL can activate." When detractors outweigh contributors, learners can self-activate SRL by recruiting assets to flip the ratio. The construct extends Kahn's psychological availability to learning contexts and adds an intraindividual summation process.
requirements: Learners must surpass a personal minimal threshold of contributors relative to detractors before SRL processes can initiate and be sustained
constraints: The framework is proposed theoretically; the article presents no empirical test of the ratio or threshold
target_learners: Adolescent and adult learners in academic settings
target_learning_goals: Initiating and sustaining self-regulated engagement in academic tasks under suboptimal conditions
examples: Sarah's scenario: a learner who cleared her desk, met bodily needs, and set intent to study was rendered unavailable by a loud noise, illustrating how environmental detractors can overwhelm antecedent preparation
key_sources: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5

article_title: How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics
citation: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169
title: Avoid normative feedback in educational practice; prefer self-referential, task- and process-level feedback
description: The authors conclude that "normative feedback should be avoided in educational practices" because even a single instance of positive or negative normative feedback affected students' emotions, performance and self-concept in largely undesirable ways. They recommend self-referential feedback comparing performance to students' own past performance, and feedback aimed at the task- and process-level that provides specific information on how to improve skills, which fosters positive achievement emotions like hope and enjoyment and makes students experience control.
requirements: Feedback should provide specific information on how to improve skills and be delivered within a responsive teacher-student relation, per the article's recommendations
constraints: The article notes negative feedback can still offer hope for improvement only when it meets the requirements of constructive criticism; long-term effects of repeated normative feedback remain unstudied
target_learning_goals: protecting achievement emotions
maintaining math self-concept
sustaining math performance
examples: In the experiment, students receiving negative normative feedback showed more anxiety and less enjoyment and hope than controls, and positive feedback diminished pre-existing low math self-concepts
key_sources: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169

article_title: Autonomy and competence frustration in young adolescent classrooms: Different associations with active and passive disengagement
citation: Stephen R. Earl, Ian M. Taylor, Carla Meijen and Louis Passfield (2016). Autonomy and Competence Frustration in Young Adolescent Classrooms: Different Associations with Active and Passive Disengagement. Learning and Instruction, 49, 32-40. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.12.001
title: Avoid psychologically controlling strategies in the classroom to prevent both active and passive disengagement
description: The article recommends that teachers refrain from psychologically controlling tactics such as guilt induction, criticism and suppressing pupil opinion, because these thwart autonomy and competence and were associated with both disengagement pathways. It states that "teacher directed interventions may be required to help teachers understand the consequences of employing psychological control and methods to avoid such strategies". Teachers are advised to demonstrate relevance and invite pupil opinion instead.
requirements: Teachers must be able to recognise controlling language and tactics in their own practice, which the authors say may require targeted interventions.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional, so causal benefits of removing control are not established by this study.
target_learning_goals: Classroom engagement and reducing active and passive disengagement
examples: The study measured pupil perceptions of teacher psychological control with items such as "My teacher does not allow me to work at my own pace" and linked those perceptions to need frustration and disengagement.
key_sources: Stephen R. Earl, Ian M. Taylor, Carla Meijen and Louis Passfield (2016). Autonomy and Competence Frustration in Young Adolescent Classrooms: Different Associations with Active and Passive Disengagement. Learning and Instruction, 49, 32-40. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.12.001

article_title: Multimedia effects during retrieval practice: Images that reveal the answer reduce vocabulary learning.
citation: van den Broek, G., Van Gog, T., Jansen, E., Pleijsant, M., & Kester, L. (2021). Multimedia Effects During Retrieval Practice: Images That Reveal the Answer Reduce Vocabulary Learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(8), 1587-1608. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000499
title: Avoid informative images during vocabulary retrieval practice because they can harm learning
description: The article concludes that during vocabulary retrieval practice, "informative images are thus potentially harmful and students have limited insight into these effects." The principle is to omit images that help learners retrieve the answer during practice, or present them only after the retrieval attempt, because such images reduce later recall while inflating feelings of competence.
requirements: Retrieval practice of vocabulary items where the image could reveal or hint at the answer
constraints: Findings come from secondary education classroom experiments on foreign vocabulary with posttests 1 to 4 days after practice
target_learners: secondary education students learning foreign vocabulary
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of foreign vocabulary
examples: In the experiments, images that helped students retrieve the answer weakened posttest recall relative to no images or images after the retrieval attempt.
key_sources: van den Broek, G., Van Gog, T., Jansen, E., Pleijsant, M., & Kester, L. (2021). Multimedia Effects During Retrieval Practice: Images That Reveal the Answer Reduce Vocabulary Learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(8), 1587-1608. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000499

article_title: A Significant Conference Report on Sex Education.
citation: New Publications, The Journal of Educational Psychology. (1920). https://journals.apa.org/edp/
title: Avoid rigidly dividing a lesson period into fixed minutes per activity, since fixed time allocation may formalize the lesson
description: This principle cautions against lesson plans that bind each activity to a fixed number of minutes. The reviewer of a 7th-grade lesson scheme, which allocated a 50-minute period across review, assignment, silent study, oral expression, and summary, suggests that to assign periods of different kinds of work within the class hour "may quite completely formalize the lesson." Flexible use of lesson time is implied as preferable.
requirements: A lesson plan whose activities would otherwise be pinned to fixed per-activity minute allocations within one period.
constraints: The caution rests on questions the reviewer raises from his own experiment in fifth grade social studies; no results of that experiment are reported.
target_learning_goals: maintaining flexible, non-formulaic lesson structure in secondary classroom teaching
examples: The reviewed proposal's allocation of a 50-minute period: 9 minutes review, 10 minutes assignment, 6 minutes silent study, 20 minutes oral expression, and 5 minutes summary, against which the reviewer states the caution.
key_sources: New Publications, The Journal of Educational Psychology. (1920). https://journals.apa.org/edp/

article_title: An inquiry into the statistical basis of a conclusion concerning sex differences.
citation: Frasier, George W. (1915). An Inquiry Into the Statistical Basis of a Conclusion Concerning Sex Differences. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Do not base conclusions about group differences on modal values of small, arbitrarily grouped distributions
description: The article argues that a modal value is sensitive to the arbitrary size and position of class intervals, quoting Rugg that the modal value "depends, within a certain range over the scale, upon the size and position of class-intervals." Group comparisons should instead use measures such as the arithmetic mean and refined median with their probable errors, and should rest on adequate numbers of cases.
requirements: Distributions must be checked under alternative class-interval sizes and positions before interpreting modes
Comparisons of central tendency should be reported with measures of dispersion such as the P.E.
constraints: The demonstration concerns a single 53-child Point Scale dataset; the article states no attempt was made to justify the interval of eight used in one illustration
target_learners: ten-year-old school children assessed on mental ability scales
target_learning_goals: fair evaluation of individual test results across sex groups
examples: The article regrouped the Yerkes monograph data with shifted five-point intervals and with eight-point intervals, showing the ten-point modal separation shrink to five points and then disappear, and compared mean (63.9 vs 60.8) and median (65.8 vs 59.7) differences with their probable errors.
key_sources: Frasier, George W. (1915). An Inquiry Into the Statistical Basis of a Conclusion Concerning Sex Differences. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients. (A Case Study.).
citation: Lincoln, Edward A. (1922). The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients (A Case Study). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 14, 484-495. https://archive.org/details/journalofeducat14
title: Classify a child's intelligence on the basis of several averaged IQ examinations plus a scientific case study, not a single test
description: The article argues that a single intelligence examination should not ground a definite classification because measurement conditions can never be identical between testings and performance fluctuates. It recommends that "no definite classification should be made on the basis of one examination alone, but that a number of Intelligence Quotients should be obtained and averaged for each individual," and closes that discrepancies increase the IQ's usefulness "providing always that a scientific case study of the individual is made." This functions as a testing-practice design principle: repeated measurement plus contextual case study yields more trustworthy classification.
requirements: Multiple examinations of the same individual at different times
Supplementary data such as teacher reports, physical measurements and examination records for the case study
constraints: Identical testing conditions are impossible because prior examination itself changes the subject and time lapses between testings
target_learners: children being examined for intelligence classification
children not getting along in school work
target_learning_goals: accurate and fair educational classification and placement
examples: The study interprets discrepancies across four years of summer-school testing and sixteen clinic retestings to show why single-exam classification is risky
key_sources: Lincoln, Edward A. (1922). The Constancy of Intelligence Quotients (A Case Study). The Journal of Educational Psychology, 14, 484-495. https://archive.org/details/journalofeducat14

article_title: Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing
citation: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7
title: Subprocess account of audio-visual associative learning as a candidate locus of dyslexia difficulty
description: The article motivates reinterpreting AV learning difficulties in dyslexia in terms of the subprocesses that could be affected: forming clear unimodal representations, binding newly associated auditory and visual information in working memory, and consolidating bound representations in long-term memory. The authors state that forming AV pairs "could be considered to rely on the process of binding in working memory, that is the integration of a number of isolated characteristics into a compound representation". Any of these subprocesses could potentially be impaired in children with DD, and domain-general skills such as attentional resources are likely candidates supporting them.
requirements: Clear representations of both auditory and visual stimuli must be available; the binding must be coded and maintained first in working memory before consolidation in long-term memory
constraints: The article notes poorer nonspeech-sound discrimination in DD has been reported in the past but with mixed evidence; further characterization of auditory processing difficulties and of the domain-general skills involved in each subprocess is needed
target_learners: Children with developmental dyslexia and typically-developing readers
target_learning_goals: Forming durable audio-visual associations through repeated exposure
examples: The article cites prior hypotheses of a failure to deploy attentional resources in cross-modal binding in developmental dyslexia, and an adult study linking learning performance to verbal working memory across two language groups
key_sources: Pasqualotto, A., Cochrane, A., Venuti, P. et al. (2025). Impaired audio-visual associations in dyslexia: evidence beyond linguistic processing. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00382-7

article_title: Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence
citation: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w
title: Avoid discarding trials as practice trials; use time-sensitive analyses instead
description: The article recommends that researchers "should avoid discarding trials whenever possible", because removing early trials as practice replaces one stationarity assumption with another unprincipled one and, as the results show, is "actually discarding signal, not noise". Instead, time-sensitive analyses of pilot data can identify timescales of change and what amount of practice would leave participants at reasonably stable performance.
requirements: Time-sensitive (trajectory) modeling of performance, or pilot data analyzed with time-sensitive methods to establish stable-performance timescales
constraints: Where practice-trial removal is still implemented, the article notes it is unclear how many trials should be removed to ensure the remaining sample is stationary
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of cognitive constructs in experimental and individual-differences research
examples: The study modeled all 68 spatial-span trials fully disaggregated (every mouse click a data line) rather than dropping early trials
key_sources: Aaron Cochrane and C. Shawn Green. (2021). Trajectories of performance change indicate multiple dissociable links between working memory and fluid intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00111-w

article_title: Beware the myth: learning styles affect parents’, children’s, and teachers’ thinking about children’s academic potential
citation: Xin Sun, Owen Norton and Shaylene E. Nancekivell. (2023). Beware the myth: learning styles affect parents', children's, and teachers' thinking about children's academic potential. npj Science of Learning 8:46. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00190-x
title: Be wary of describing children as hands-on or visual learners because these descriptions trigger unwarranted inferences about ability
description: The article recommends caution in labeling students by learning style. It argues that "these categories, similar to other social categories, are likely to trigger incorrect thinking about children's abilities by educators, parents, and their peers", even when descriptions are used with good intentions. The recommendation follows directly from the three experiments showing such descriptions shape judgments of intelligence, sportiness, effort, and predicted grades.
requirements: Describing a child to parents, teachers, or peers using a learning style category such as visual or hands-on is sufficient to trigger the inferred ability differences shown in the experiments.
constraints: The evidence comes from American, predominately white samples of parents, teachers, and 6–12-year-old children; the authors state the effect's real-world magnitude may differ because surveys used forced-choice decisions.
How labels versus descriptions influence the effects is an open question for future work.
target_learners: elementary school students (grades K–12, children 6–12 years studied)
target_learning_goals: accurate adult and peer judgments of children's academic potential and subject-specific abilities
examples: In Experiment 3, parents and teachers given descriptions of a Grade-5 visual and a hands-on learner predicted the visual learner would earn higher grades in math, language arts, and social studies, and the hands-on learner higher grades in art, gym, and music.
key_sources: Xin Sun, Owen Norton and Shaylene E. Nancekivell. (2023). Beware the myth: learning styles affect parents', children's, and teachers' thinking about children's academic potential. npj Science of Learning 8:46. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00190-x

article_title: Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching
citation: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1
title: AVW-Space active video watching platform
description: AVW-Space is a controlled video watching learning environment designed for self-study, in which teachers select publicly available videos and define aspects that serve as micro-scaffolds for learning. It comprises a Private Space, where students individually watch videos and write comments linked to a video timestamp and an aspect, and a Social Space, where teacher-approved anonymised comments can be browsed and rated using reflection-promoting categories. The article states: "AVW-Space fosters active learning via interactive note taking and by providing micro-scaffolds for reflection", and students can also rate comments written by others, providing opportunities for social learning. The instantiation for pitch presentations included eight YouTube videos (four tutorials and four example pitch presentations).
requirements: Teacher effort to select videos and define aspects; teacher approval of comments before sharing in the Social Space
constraints: The version used in the reported studies could not analyse comment text, so Active and Constructive learners were not distinguished
target_learning_goals: transferable skills, specifically delivering pitch presentations
examples: Aspects for tutorials included reflective triggers such as "I didn't realize I wasn't doing this" and "I did/saw this in the past"; example-video aspects were Delivery, Speech, Structure and Visual aids
key_sources: Vania Dimitrova & Antonija Mitrovic. (2021). Choice Architecture for Nudges to Support Constructive Learning in Active Video Watching. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00263-1

article_title: The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study
citation: Kogan, G., Chassidim, H., & Rabaev, I. (2024). The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10382-w
title: AVDS: a free online animation and visualization tool for data structures
description: The AVDS tool is a free online animation and visualization tool developed to complement an undergraduate Data Structures course, covering "a classic set of algorithms and data structures commonly studied in the undergraduate data structures course." It provides interactive visualization of algorithm execution, including AVL tree rotations. Source code is available on GitHub, and the tool provides usage reports for teaching staff showing analytics per topic.
requirements: Requires JavaScript, HTML, and CSS programming experience to understand the source code
constraints: At the time of the experiment, the system did not show the steps of the algorithm, but did provide a final answer only
target_learners: undergraduate computer science and software engineering students
target_learning_goals: understanding data structures and algorithms, including AVL tree operations
examples: Used during a 20-minute performance test on AVL trees; students could use it to solve questions or verify answers
key_sources: Kogan, G., Chassidim, H., & Rabaev, I. (2024). The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10382-w

article_title: Training film evaluation: Comparison between two films on personal hygiene: TF8–155 and TF8–1665
citation: No author line printed. (1953). Training Film Evaluation: Comparison Between Two Films On Personal Hygiene: TF8-155 and TF8-1665. Audio-Visual Communication Review digest of Instructional Film Research Program technical reports. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Do not use the singing-commercial approach in training films, because it costs more, takes more production time, and is no more effective than straightforward presentation
description: A design recommendation from the VanderMeer comparison of two personal hygiene training films for military trainees. The singing-commercial approach with strong personal appeals was more expensive and slower to produce, yet produced no better learning, behavior change, or motivation than straightforward presentation of the facts to be learned. The report recommended that "the 'singing commercial' approach should not be used in training films."
requirements: Training films whose goal is to change hygiene habits, knowledge, and attitudes of trainees
constraints: Recommendation rests on one comparison with 176 Army recruits on personal hygiene content
target_learning_goals: personal hygiene habits, knowledge, and attitudes
examples: The comparison pitted TF8-155, a singing-commercial film with strong personal appeals, against the less costly TF8-1665 using a straightforward instructional approach
key_sources: No author line printed. (1953). Training Film Evaluation: Comparison Between Two Films On Personal Hygiene: TF8-155 and TF8-1665. Audio-Visual Communication Review digest of Instructional Film Research Program technical reports. https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: A study of the audio-visual administrative and supervisory functions in selected schools of vocational and adult education in wisconsin
citation: AUDIO-VISUAL ADMINISTRATION. Abstract of Barnard, David P. A Study of the Audio-Visual Administrative and Supervisory Functions in Selected Schools of Vocational and Adult Education in Wisconsin. Doctor's thesis, Indiana University. Audio-Visual Communication Review. (1955). https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Audio-visual services require administration and supervision by trained personnel
description: The article's first recommendation is that schools "recognize that audio-visual services require the administration and supelwision of trained personnel." The principle holds that AV functions cannot run themselves: without designated, trained coordinators and operational plans, services lapse, as the study's documented deficits show. It underpins the author's call to employ well-prepared, dynamic audio-visual coordinators.
requirements: Employ well-prepared, dynamic audio-visual coordinators
Develop operational plans for audio-visual administration and supervision
constraints: Derived from conditions observed in Wisconsin vocational and adult education schools
target_learning_goals: organized, supervised audio-visual service delivery supporting instruction
examples: The study found coordinators lacked sufficient time and that no organized procedures existed for previewing, evaluating, and selecting materials, supporting the need for trained administrative personnel.

A Study of the Audio-Visual Administrative and Supervisory Functions in Selected Schools of Vocational and Adult Education in Wisconsin. Doctor's thesis, Indiana University. article_title: Flipped @ SBU: Student Satisfaction and the College Classroom
citation: Gross, B., Hoffman, M., Marinari, M., DeSimone, K., & Burke, P. (2015). Flipped @ SBU: Student satisfaction and the college classroom. Educational Research Quarterly, 39(2), 37-52.
title: Instructors new to a topic area should avoid flipping their course until they have more teaching experience.
description: The authors report that flipped courses require considerable extra preparation throughout the semester, and all instructors in the study agreed that instructors new to a topic area should delay flipping. This principle reflects their direct experience across three disciplines during the study.
requirements: Instructor familiarity with the course content and teaching context before adopting the flipped format
constraints: Based on instructor self-report at a single institution; the authors note "a considerable amount of extra preparation required of the instructor throughout the semester"
target_learning_goals: Effective implementation of flipped course design
examples: All instructors in the study agreed that "an instructor new to teaching a topic area should probably avoid flipping their course until they have more experience."
key_sources: Gross, B., Hoffman, M., Marinari, M., DeSimone, K., & Burke, P. (2015). Flipped @ SBU: Student satisfaction and the college classroom. Educational Research Quarterly, 39(2), 37-52. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1166718

article_title: Pinch Hitter: The Effectiveness of Content Summaries Delivered by a Guest Lecturer in Online Course Videos
citation: Fanguy, M., Costley, J., & Baldwin, M. (2017). Pinch Hitter: The Effectiveness of Content Summaries Delivered by a Guest Lecturer in Online Course Videos. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 18(7). http://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl/article/view/3210
title: Avoid abrupt scene changes in video lectures for flipped classrooms and e-learning environments
description: Drawing on their own finding that the guest-lecturer condition with scene changes underperformed, and citing Kim et al. (2014), the authors advise video developers to avoid abrupt scene changes. They state that "avoiding abrupt scene changes in video lectures appears to be sound advice for video content developers for flipped classrooms, MOOCs, and other e-learning environments, and this suggestion was confirmed in the present study."
requirements: Video content developers should keep the same background throughout summary segments
constraints: The study could not isolate the guest-lecturer effect from the scene-change effect
target_learning_goals: recall of video lecture content
examples: In the study, only the guest-lecturer condition contained scene changes from a slide background to a coffee shop setting and back again, while the summaries-only group kept the same slide background throughout.
key_sources: Fanguy, M., Costley, J., & Baldwin, M. (2017). Pinch Hitter: The Effectiveness of Content Summaries Delivered by a Guest Lecturer in Online Course Videos. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 18(7). http://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl/article/view/3210

article_title: Improving English Learners' Productive Collocation Knowledge: The Effects of Involvement Load, Spacing, and Intentionality
citation: Snoder, P. (2017). Improving English Learners’ Productive Collocation Knowledge: The Effects of Involvement Load, Spacing, and Intentionality. TESL Canada Journal, 34(3). https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1277
title: Avoid original-sentence-writing when the goal is reproducing collocation form
description: The authors state that "original-sentence-writing cannot be recommended if instructors aim to help learners reproduce the form of new collocations", because semantic elaboration of word meaning may come at the expense of learning word form (lex-IP theory). Task D, which combined dictionary search and sentence writing, produced the lowest gains. They instead point to contrastive analysis and translation as the best current recommendation.
requirements: Instructors must have a clear goal: this applies when the target is productive form recall
constraints: The recommendation concerns form reproduction; the authors note a receptive meaning test might have favoured Task D
target_learning_goals: productive collocation form knowledge
examples: Task D participants searched dictionary entries then wrote original sentences; this task scored lowest (M = 2.66 of 7)
key_sources: Snoder, P. (2017). Improving English Learners’ Productive Collocation Knowledge: The Effects of Involvement Load, Spacing, and Intentionality. TESL Canada Journal, 34(3). https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1277

article_title: Punchline with(out) purpose: Integrating research on instructional humour and seductive details.
citation: Bender, L., Renkl, A., & Endres, T. (2026). Punchline with(out) purpose: Integrating research on instructional humour and seductive details. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70080
title: Avoid irrelevant instructional humour because of the risk of a detrimental seductive details effect
description: Based on the finding that course-related humour without a cognitive function impaired transfer (Study 1) and recall (Study 2) relative to relevant humour, and impaired transfer relative to no humour in Study 1, the authors conclude it may be safer to avoid irrelevant instructional humour even when it is course-related. This recommendation integrates seductive details research with instructional humour research.
requirements: Distinguish humour that illustrates or clarifies learning content from humour that merely entertains
constraints: The seductive details effect versus control was not consistently replicated in Study 2
target_learning_goals: learning performance
transfer
examples: In Study 1, the irrelevant-humour group's transfer performance was significantly worse than the control group's (M diff = −8.63, p = .018).
key_sources: Bender, L., Renkl, A., & Endres, T. (2026). Punchline with(out) purpose: Integrating research on instructional humour and seductive details. The British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70080

article_title: Smiling and first impressions in ad hoc entrustment decisions: An avatar-based simulation study.
citation: Bauermann Moritz, Schindler Ann-Kathrin, Kuchenbaur Marco, Rühl Jasmin, Reinert Patrick, Kunz Miriam, Friedrich-Welz Sarah, André Elisabeth, Rotthoff Thomas. (2026). Smiling and first impressions in ad hoc entrustment decisions: An avatar-based simulation study. GMS Journal for Medical Education 43(2): Doc16. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume43/zma001810
title: Avatar-based ad hoc entrustment simulation with 36 clinical scenarios and FACSGen-animated expressions
description: A cost-effective online simulation paradigm for studying entrustment decisions: participants read 36 narrative clinical entrustment scenarios in randomized order and viewed two 5-second avatar videos per scenario, deciding dichotomously whether to entrust the task and rating trustworthiness on a 4-point Likert scale (0 to 3). "The trustees were represented by avatars. After each scenario, the participants viewed two 5-second videos of these avatars." Facial expressions (Duchenne smile, neutral) were standardized using FACSGen action units; 18 female and 18 male avatars were each shown once per expression.
requirements: Standardized facial expressions animated via Facial Action Coding System action units for clarity and reproducibility.
constraints: The authors note avatar realism was limited by FACS compatibility restrictions, which limited reproducibility and standardization of expressions; only avatars' heads were designed to focus on facial expressions.
target_learning_goals: ad hoc entrustment decision-making within the entrustable professional activities framework
key_sources: Bauermann Moritz, Schindler Ann-Kathrin, Kuchenbaur Marco, Rühl Jasmin, Reinert Patrick, Kunz Miriam, Friedrich-Welz Sarah, André Elisabeth, Rotthoff Thomas. (2026). Smiling and first impressions in ad hoc entrustment decisions: An avatar-based simulation study. GMS Journal for Medical Education 43(2): Doc16. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume43/zma001810

article_title: Early morning university classes are associated with impaired sleep and academic performance.
citation: Yeo Sing Chen, Lai Clin K. Y., Tan Jacinda, Lim Samantha, Chandramoghan Yuvan, Tan Teck Kiang, Gooley Joshua J. (2023). Early morning university classes are associated with impaired sleep and academic performance. Nature Human Behaviour. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01531-x
title: Universities should consider avoiding mandatory early morning classes and schedule classes later in the day
description: The article concludes that universities should consider "avoiding mandatory early morning classes", because students are more likely to miss class, get less sleep and obtain a lower grade point average with early starts. It proposes scheduling classes later and making classrooms a shared resource across departments, using archived digital traces to assess scheduling impacts on students.
requirements: A scalable method for assessing the impact of class scheduling practices on student behaviour, such as the archived Wi-Fi and LMS digital traces analysed in the article
constraints: The supporting evidence is observational and did not establish causality
Some students may gradually shift their bedtime later, reducing the benefit of later start times
target_learning_goals: class attendance
healthy sleep behaviour
academic achievement (grade point average)
examples: Wi-Fi connection logs, LMS login data and actigraphy were used to quantify attendance, sleep opportunities and grade point average associations across class start times at the university
key_sources: Yeo Sing Chen, Lai Clin K. Y., Tan Jacinda, Lim Samantha, Chandramoghan Yuvan, Tan Teck Kiang, Gooley Joshua J. (2023). Early morning university classes are associated with impaired sleep and academic performance. Nature Human Behaviour. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01531-x

article_title: Transferability of robotic console skills by early robotic surgeons: a multi-platform crossover trial of simulation training.
citation: Larkins Kirsten M., Mohan Helen M., Gray Matthew, Costello Daniel M., Costello Anthony J., Heriot Alexander G., Warrier Satish K. (2022). Transferability of robotic console skills by early robotic surgeons: a multi-platform crossover trial of simulation training. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-022-01475-w
title: Aviation type-rating model as a framework for multi-platform robotic surgical training and credentialing
description: The article draws an analogy between robotic surgical training and aviation credentialling across different aircraft, described as type rating. In aviation, type rating is "an approved and standardised course of training which upon successful completion; the pilot is qualified to fly a particular type of aircraft", involving simulator exercises, recurrent training, line checks and maintenance of recency to avoid skills fade. Manufacturers design aircraft for similarity to allow cross-licensing, and the article suggests robotic platforms may similarly be cross-credentialed when risk metrics show they are not dissimilar enough to cause harm.
requirements: Standardised training courses per platform type
Recurrent training and recency requirements to prevent skills fade
Assessment of platform similarity based on operation feel, console similarities and critical risk management
constraints: Robotic surgical training standards have not yet reached the example set in the aviation industry
The decision-making behind cross-licensing similar aircraft is complex and only analogous
target_learners: early robotic surgeons training across multiple robotic operating platforms
target_learning_goals: safe and proficient console operation across multiple robotic platforms
examples: The article likens robotic operating systems to aircraft with similar potential for harm when poorly operated, and proposes proficiency-based type rating for each robotic type
key_sources: Larkins Kirsten M., Mohan Helen M., Gray Matthew, Costello Daniel M., Costello Anthony J., Heriot Alexander G., Warrier Satish K. (2022). Transferability of robotic console skills by early robotic surgeons: a multi-platform crossover trial of simulation training. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-022-01475-w

article_title: Doctoral physical therapy students’ increased confidence following exploration of active video gaming systems in a problem-based learning curriculum in the United States: a pre- and post-intervention study.
citation: Wormley Michelle Elizabeth, Romney Wendy, Veneri Diana, Oberlander Andrea. (2022). Doctoral physical therapy students' increased confidence following exploration of active video gaming systems in a problem-based learning curriculum in the United States: a pre- and post-intervention study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2022.19.7
title: AVG laboratory rotation in which students role-play both patient and therapist across diagnosis-based stations
description: A reusable lab design in which students rotate through small-group stations, each built around a patient case with a specific functional level and AVG system. "Students acted as the patient to appreciate game operation, physical requirements, and level of difficulty. They also approached each station as the therapist to practice guarding skills, cueing, monitoring, modifying and considering exercise prescription". Stations were followed by a faculty-facilitated full-class debrief with guiding questions, embedded across two consecutive semesters of a PBL curriculum.
requirements: Faculty facilitators at each station
Patient cases already familiar from PBL tutorials
AVG systems and games matched to patient functional levels (stability, mobility, mobility plus)
constraints: Described and evaluated in a single DPT program at one university in the Northeast United States
target_learning_goals: confidence using active video gaming as a physical therapy intervention
guarding, cueing, and exercise prescription skills
examples: Lab activity #1 used three stations: a 73-yr female post-stroke (Nintendo Wii), an 82-yr female with Parkinson's disease (Nintendo Switch), and a 27-yr male post-concussion (Xbox One Kinect), each 45 minutes with a 30-minute debrief.

article_title: OSCE rater cognition - an international multi-centre qualitative study.
citation: Hyde Sarah, Fessey Christine, Boursicot Katharine, MacKenzie Rhoda, McGrath Deirdre. (2022). OSCE rater cognition – an international multi-centre qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-03077-w
title: Do not prioritise objectivity above context by insisting examiners disregard their own experience and stick rigidly to a rating schema
description: Because raters' idiosyncratic judgements arise from reasoned attempts to compensate for perceived OSCE inauthenticity, forcing strict checklist adherence is counterproductive: "Prioritising objectivity above context by trying to insist that examiners disregard their own experience and stick rigidly to a schema is likely to be unhelpful." The article also notes extensive checklists can cause cognitive overload and push examiners to rely on memory or prioritise idiosyncratic elements. Assessment design should instead acknowledge examiners' experience and the method's limitations.
requirements: Awareness among assessment designers of the limitations of the assessment method and its consequences for student and assessor behaviour
constraints: Raters in this study were aware they were deviating from instruction and felt justified, so the authors judge such behaviour difficult to change
target_learners: OSCE examiners and medical educators designing rater-based assessment
target_learning_goals: fair and defensible clinical competence assessment
examples: Experienced examiners in the study reported weighting their 'favourite things' more or less than the checklist in front of them, and overriding marking for candidates they judged genuine
